spec.description: The CPU and the memory each Flowrensic server uses, against the limits of its container. A server that stays near its limits for long gets slow and may stop. The whole row has no data only when the server cannot read its container, for example outside a container on macOS, where only the use shows and no limit line.

options.content: The CPU and the memory of the container of each server against its limits.

spec.title: CPU used against the CPU limit by instance
spec.description: CPU each server uses, in cores: 1 is one full core. Three lines show the lowest, the average and the highest use of each minute, the way ECS shows CPUUtilization. The top line is the CPU limit of the container, the cores it may use. The line below it is where Flowrensic starts to count the CPU as too high, 90% of the limit by default. Normal: the use stays well under that line. Bad: the use stays above it for 5 minutes, then Flowrensic raises a finding about itself and may shed load. On ECS the use is the whole task, a collector container too, against the task's limit. A server with no CPU limit, for example outside a container, shows the use alone, with no limit lines.

spec.title: Memory used against the memory limit by instance
spec.description: Memory each server uses, in bytes. The top line is the memory limit of the container. The line below it is where Flowrensic starts to count the memory as too high, 90% of the limit by default. Normal: the use stays well under that line. Bad: the use stays above it for 5 minutes, then Flowrensic raises a finding about itself; at the limit the container is stopped for lack of memory. On ECS the use is the whole task against the task's limit. A server with no memory limit shows the use alone, with no limit lines.

spec.title: Times throttled per second by instance
spec.description: How many times per second the container of each server hit its CPU limit and had to wait. Normal: 0 or close to it. Bad: a line that stays above 0, the server wants more CPU than it may use and gets slower. No data on ECS Fargate: AWS caps the CPU by the size of the task and gives no throttled count, so this panel stays empty there and the CPU panel is the one to read. No data either on a server with no CPU limit, for example outside a container.

Whether each server sheds load to protect itself, and which of its health numbers are over their limit now. A health number is one of the numbers a server measures about itself: CPU, memory, time waited for a database connection, database connections, request time, requests running and work waiting of a job. Over its limit means it stayed above its limit for a while, 5 minutes by default. Whether a job is paused or slowed shows in the section of that job. The whole row has no data on a server that does not shed load or does not check its limits.

options.content: Whether each server sheds load, and which of the numbers it measures about its own health are over their limit now. Whether a job is paused or slowed shows in the section of that job. Over its limit means a number stayed above its limit for a while, for example CPU over 90% for 5 minutes.

spec.title: Stage of shedding by instance
spec.description: The stage of shedding of each server, a number from 0 to 3. 0 none, everything runs. 1 background jobs are paused. 2 bulk requests are refused too. 3 normal requests are refused too; urgent requests are always answered. Normal: 0. Bad: above 0, the server is over a limit and protects itself; each stage starts after the one before it did not help for a minute, by default. No data on a server that does not shed load, when shedding is turned off.

spec.title: Health numbers over their limit now by instance
spec.description: How many parts of each health number are over their limit now on each server, 0 when none is. A part is a database pool, a kind of request or a job. The lines: cpu is CPU used, memory is memory used, pool_wait is the time waited for a database connection, connections is the database connections of all servers, call_time is how long requests take, calls_running is the requests running at once, work_waiting is the work waiting for a job, and backlog_growing is work waiting that keeps growing. Normal: every line at 0. Bad: a line above 0, the findings of the Findings row name the part, the limit and the value. A health number whose limit is off stays at 0. No data on a server that does not check its limits.

The requests each server answers, by kind and by priority, how long they take, and the requests it refuses while it sheds load. A kind of request is one call of the Flowrensic API, such as ListThresholds. The priority is urgent, normal or bulk.

options.content: The requests each server answers, by kind and by priority, and the requests it refuses while it sheds load.

spec.title: Requests running now by kind of request by instance
spec.description: Requests each server is answering right now, a count, one line for each kind of request. The flat line is the limit of requests running at once, the same for every kind. Normal: low numbers that go up and down. Bad: a line that keeps going up, requests arrive faster than the server finishes them; above the limit for 5 minutes Flowrensic raises a finding. No limit line while the limit is off, which is the default.

spec.title: Requests per second by priority by instance
spec.description: Requests per second each server got, by priority: urgent, normal and bulk, both the answered and the refused ones. Requests with no priority, like the health check and the metrics endpoint, are not counted. Use it to see what load the server gets, next to the refused requests. There is no limit and no good or bad value of its own. No data on a server that does not shed load, when shedding is turned off.

spec.title: Request time p95 by kind of request by instance
spec.description: The time in seconds in which 95% of the requests of each kind finished, over the last few minutes. The flat line is the request time limit, 1 second by default, checked for each kind on its own. Normal: well under the line. Bad: a kind that stays above the line for 5 minutes, then Flowrensic raises a finding about itself. This panel works the time out over a longer window than the check does, so a line near the limit is a hint and the finding is what counts. No limit line while the limit is off. No line for a kind with no requests.

spec.title: Requests refused per second by priority by instance
spec.description: Requests per second each server refused while it shed load, by priority: bulk at stage 2 and above, normal at stage 3. Urgent requests are never refused. Normal: 0. Bad: above 0, callers get errors and have to try again later; see the Shedding row for why. No data on a server that does not shed load, when shedding is turned off.
The connections of each server to Postgres, the time it waited for a free connection, and the connections of all servers together against the most Postgres allows.

options.content: The connections of each server to Postgres, the time it waited for one, and the connections of all servers.

spec.title: Database connections in use and free by pool by instance
spec.description: Connections of each database pool of each server, a count, split into in use and free. Each server has a few pools, one for each kind of work. Normal: some connections free most of the time. Bad: a pool with 0 free for long, work waits for a connection; the next panel shows how long. There is no limit line, the size of each pool is its limit.

spec.title: Time waited for a connection per second by pool by instance
spec.description: Seconds that work waited for a free connection of each pool, per second. 0.5 means that, together, work waited half a second in each second. The flat line is the limit of the time waited, 0.5 by default, the same for every pool. Normal: 0 or close to it. Bad: a pool that stays above the line for 5 minutes, the pool is too small for the work, and Flowrensic raises a finding about itself. No limit line while the limit is off.

spec.title: Connections of all servers against max_connections
spec.description: Connections all Flowrensic servers hold on Postgres together, a count. The top line is max_connections of Postgres, the most it allows. The line below it is where Flowrensic starts to count the connections as too many, 80% of max_connections by default. Normal: well under that line. Bad: above it for 5 minutes, new servers or new pools may soon be refused by Postgres, and Flowrensic raises a finding about itself. No limit line below the top while the limit is off.

One section for each background job of the server, such as the puller, the findings job or retention, so a job added later gets its own section with no change to the dashboard. A job that runs once per namespace, like the puller, has one section, with the largest of its namespaces. A job gets its section once it ended its first pass; a job stuck in its first pass has one only on the server that runs the findings job.

options.content: One section for each background job the server reports, so a job added later gets its own. A job that runs once per namespace, like the puller, has one section.

spec.title: Work waiting of $job by instance
spec.description: The work this job still has to do after its last pass, in the unit this job counts, such as runs for the puller, histories for the findings job or bytes for retention. Of a job that runs once per namespace it is the largest namespace. The flat line is the work waiting limit of this job, checked for each namespace. Normal: low, or going back down after each pass. Bad: above the line for 5 minutes, or a line that keeps growing, the job does not keep up, and Flowrensic raises a finding about itself. No limit line while the limit is off, which is the default for every job.

spec.title: Last pass of $job against its interval by instance
spec.description: How long the last pass of this job took, in seconds, the longest of its namespaces, and its interval as a flat line, the time between two passes. Normal: well under the interval line. Bad: a pass above the line took longer than its interval, so the job falls behind. No data until the job ended its first pass.

spec.title: State of $job by instance
spec.description: The state of this job on each server, one line for each of behind, late, paused and slowed. Behind and late count how many namespaces of the job are behind or late. Paused is 1 while shedding pauses the job, slowed is 1 while the job runs only one pass in a number of passes: for the stored rules and replay rules jobs because another job is behind, for the puller, findings and retention jobs because CPU or the database is busy, as the panel beside it shows. Normal: every line at 0. Bad: behind or late above 0, the job does not keep up, and the Findings row shows it. Behind and late show above 0 only on the server that runs the findings job, since that job judges every server; on the other servers they stay at 0.

spec.title: Why $job is slowed by instance
spec.description: Why this job is slowed on each server, one line for each busy signal: cpu, the CPU used over the last minute above its limit; pool_wait, the time waited for a database connection above its limit; connections_refused, the connections Postgres refused to a pool, a minute, above their limit; connections, the connections of all servers against max_connections above their limit; and active_queries, lock_waiting and slow_queries, the active queries, the queries waiting on locks and the slow queries of the database above the CPU limit share of its cores. A line is 1 while that signal slows the job, and 0 otherwise. A slowed job runs one pass in 4 and lets the others go, so the server and the database stay healthy. Normal: 0, or 1 for a short while. Bad: 1 for a long time, the server or the database is too small for the work. This reason slows only the puller, findings and retention jobs, so the other jobs have no line here; the stored rules and replay rules jobs are slowed only while another job is behind, which this panel does not show.
How much storage the whole install uses against its size limit, and which tables are the largest. One value for the whole install, not one for each server.

options.content: The storage of the whole install against its size limit, and the largest tables.

spec.title: Storage used against the size limit
spec.description: Storage used by the database and the history files together, in bytes, and the size limit of the store as a flat line, 10 GiB by default. Normal: well under the line. Bad: at the line, Flowrensic deletes the oldest data before its age limit to stay under it, and logs a warning for each deletion.

spec.title: The largest tables by size
spec.description: Size on disk of each of the 10 largest tables of the Flowrensic database, in bytes, with their indexes. There is no limit and no good or bad value of its own. Use it to see what fills the database when the storage panel grows.

The findings Flowrensic raised about itself, by kind. over_limit is a health number over its limit, job_backlog_growing is work waiting that keeps growing, job_behind is a job behind, and job_late is a job late. Each one is a warning, so it raises an alert too.

options.content: The findings Flowrensic raised about itself, by kind: a health number over its limit (over_limit), work waiting that keeps growing (job_backlog_growing), a job behind (job_behind) or late (job_late).

spec.title: Findings Flowrensic raised about itself by kind by instance
spec.description: How many findings about itself each server raised, by kind, in each step of the graph. Normal: no data or 0, nothing was wrong. Bad: any line above 0; open the findings in the Flowrensic UI to see the part, the limit and the value. Findings about jobs come from the server that runs the findings job.

Whether Flowrensic is catching up: pulling old runs from Temporal after it fell behind, as after a deploy that empties the database, or after new runs closed faster than it pulls them. Each namespace is reported by the server that pulls it. The Dashboard screen of the Flowrensic UI shows the same.

options.content: The catch-up of each namespace after the puller fell behind: the runs still to pull, the percent done and the time left.

spec.title: Runs left to pull by namespace
spec.description: An estimate of the runs of each namespace that Temporal holds and Flowrensic has not pulled yet, in runs. It is counted only while the namespace catches up, and is 0 once it caught up. Normal: 0, or a line that goes down to 0. Bad: a line that stays up or grows, the puller does not keep up. No data while pulling is off, and for a namespace that never fell behind.

spec.title: Catch-up done in percent by namespace
spec.description: How much of the catch-up of each namespace is done, in percent: the runs pulled since it started against those runs plus the runs left. 100 once it caught up. Normal: 100, or a line that climbs to 100. Bad: a line that stays flat under 100. No data while pulling is off, and for a namespace that never fell behind.

spec.title: Time left of the catch-up by namespace
spec.description: An estimate of the time the catch-up of each namespace still takes, in seconds: the runs left at the speed of the past runs it pulled in the last 20 minutes. 0 once it caught up. Normal: 0, or a line that goes down. Bad: a line that grows, the puller gets slower or the runs grow faster. No data while pulling is off, for a namespace that never fell behind, and while the end is not known yet, in the first poll or when nothing was pulled.

How much of its capacity Flowrensic uses, as one load number for all its work. A job uses all its capacity when its pass takes its whole interval, or when the puller finds as many runs as its fetch budget. The CPU of a server uses all of it at its CPU limit. The parts work side by side, so the load number is the highest of them. The Dashboard screen of the Flowrensic UI shows the same.

options.content: The share of its capacity Flowrensic uses: its own jobs added, each job, the requests sent to it, and the database. All work is the three added. Under 100% it keeps up, over 100% it falls behind. The CPU of each server is beside it, not part of it.

spec.title: Capacity used by all work
spec.description: The load number: the share of capacity of its own jobs, of the requests sent to it and of the database, added, in percent, the same as the Dashboard screen. The load of each instance is its own jobs, its requests and the database as it read it. 30 means Flowrensic can take about 3 times more work. Normal: under 100. Bad: over 100, Flowrensic falls behind and its backlog grows. No data before the first pass of a job ended.

spec.expr: sum(max by (task) (flowrensic_job_load_percent)) + (max(flowrensic_requests_load_percent) or vector(0)) + (max(flowrensic_db_load_percent) or vector(0))

spec.title: Capacity used by own jobs
spec.description: The share of capacity of its own jobs, every job added, and of each job, in percent. For the puller, the runs that came in for a poll against its fetch budget, never the runs left. For any other job, its last pass against its interval, the scopes a server runs added up. Normal: under 100. Bad: over 100, the job does not keep up and its work waits. No data before the first pass of a job ended.

spec.title: CPU share by instance
spec.description: The CPU each server used in the last minute against its CPU limit, in percent. Normal: under 100. Bad: near 100, the server runs short of CPU and its work slows down. No data on a server with no CPU limit, as outside a container.

spec.title: Capacity used by requests by instance
spec.description: The time the requests sent to each server ran in the last 5 seconds, Connect RPC calls, updates from the interceptor, OTLP pushes and remote writes, against the cores of the server, in percent. Normal: under 100. Bad: over 100, requests wait for each other. No data in the first second after a server starts.

spec.title: Capacity used by the database
spec.description: The share of the database, the highest of the servers, in percent: its active queries against FLOWRENSIC_DB_CORES. Every client of the database counts, not only Flowrensic. Disk reads are on the panel Database activity and are not part of the share. Normal: under 100. Bad: over 100, queries wait for a core, a lock or the disk. No data while no server could read the database.

spec.title: Database activity
spec.description: The queries running on the database now, of every client, those of them that wait for a lock, those that started more than a second ago, and the blocks it reads from outside its shared buffers a second. Normal: few active queries and none waiting. Bad: queries that wait on locks or stay slow, or disk reads that keep rising. No data while no server could read the database.

spec.title: Refused connections a minute by pool by instance
spec.description: Connections that Postgres refused to each pool of each server in the last minute, a count, for example with too many clients. The flat line is the limit of the refused connections, 1 a minute by default, the same for every pool. Normal: 0. Bad: a pool above the line for 5 minutes, Postgres has no room for the connections Flowrensic needs, its work fails and Flowrensic raises a finding about itself. No limit line while the limit is off.

spec.title: Why the catch-up is held by instance
spec.description: Why the catch-up of past runs is held on each server, one line for each signal: cpu, pool_wait, connections_refused, connections, active_queries, lock_waiting and slow_queries, the busy signals that slow the own jobs, and memory, cpu, pool_wait, connections_refused, connections and calls_running, a value that would start shedding and stayed over its limit for a while. A line is 1 while that signal holds the catch-up, and 0 otherwise. While held, the puller takes no past run, and live runs keep their pace. Normal: 0, or 1 for a short while. Bad: 1 for a long time, the catch-up does not move. No data while pulling is off.
